extracted.intended_audience: administrative law scholars, regulatory lawyers, judges, and law students
extracted.subtask_description: Analyze and describe the standards and criteria courts should apply when reviewing agency statutory interpretations after Loper Bright, including implications for stare decisis, possible replacement doctrines (Skidmore or de novo), and constitutional questions about Chevron.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chevron deference doctrine (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts defer to federal agencies’ reasonable interpretations of ambiguous statutes the agencies administer (the command from the 1984 Chevron decision).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explained as a bright-line rule that required courts to accept agency interpretations when statutes were ambiguous and the agency's interpretation was reasonable. The piece notes the Supreme Court in Loper Bright overruled Chevron and discusses how Chevron structured separation-of-powers relationships and decisionmaking practices over decades.

rubrics_metrics.name: APA's command that courts decide legal questions
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the Administrative Procedure Act, 'the reviewing court shall decide all relevant questions of law.' The Chief Justice reads this to mean no deference to agencies on legal questions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used by the majority to support the conclusion that Chevron is inconsistent with the APA. The author notes debate in scholarship about pre-APA deference doctrines and suggests the majority treats the APA text as dispositive against any judicial deference doctrine like Chevron.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independent-judgment standard for statutory interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts must exercise their independent judgment in deciding whether an agency has acted within its statutory authority; judicial review requires courts to resolve statutory ambiguities themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characterized as the replacement approach emphasized by the majority opinion: courts should not defer simply because a statute is ambiguous. The post warns independent-judgment review involves many judgment calls and may be no more 'workable' than Chevron in hard cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respecting valid delegations while policing statutory limits
rubrics_metrics.description: When a statute delegates authority to an agency consistent with constitutional limits, courts must respect that delegation while ensuring the agency acts within it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Majority language preserves the notion that valid delegations should be honored; the court still expects judges to ensure agencies stay within delegated authority, distinguishing respect for delegation from automatic deference to agency legal interpretations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agencies do not have special competence to resolve statutory ambiguities (majority view)
rubrics_metrics.description: Chevron’s presumption that Congress delegates interpretive authority to agencies is misguided because agencies have no special competence in resolving statutory ambiguities; courts do.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chief Justice Roberts argues the Framers expected courts to resolve ambiguities; the author notes disagreement with this categorical claim and references empirical and congressional-practice evidence that complicates the majority’s assertion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stare decisis treatment for judge-made deference doctrines
rubrics_metrics.description: Judge-made doctrines like Chevron receive a weaker form of precedential weight than statutory stare decisis; stare decisis analysis must consider doctrinal character, workability, and conflict with statute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The majority frames Chevron as judge-made and in conflict with the APA's plain text, justifying overruling. The post contrasts this with prior positions (e.g., Kisor) that embraced stronger stare decisis protections for deference doctrines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of prior holdings that relied on Chevron
rubrics_metrics.description: Holdings in specific cases that a particular agency action is lawful remain subject to statutory stare decisis despite doctrinal change; mere reliance on Chevron by itself is not a 'special justification' to preserve a precedent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites the majority’s attempt to limit disruption: prior case holdings that specific agency actions are lawful remain binding; but to overrule such precedents courts still need the usual special-justification standards — mere reliance on Chevron is insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Workability as a stare decisis factor
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a doctrine is workable in practice is relevant to the stare decisis analysis about whether to retain or overrule it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The majority argues Chevron is unworkable due to accumulated steps/exceptions; the author notes the replacement approach (independent judgment) may also be unworkable, and that empirical findings about Chevron’s application are contested.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reliance interests and Brand X flip‑flopping
rubrics_metrics.description: Reliance interests (e.g., agencies or regulated parties relying on prior interpretations) are limited as a justification to uphold precedents because Brand X permits agencies to change prior regulatory interpretations under Chevron.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The majority quickly rejects heavy reliance-interest claims, noting Brand X allows agencies to flip-flop and thus prior reliance does not necessarily countermine overruling Chevron. The author expresses skepticism this will fully prevent litigation upheaval.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skidmore deference factors (weight-based approach)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under Skidmore, the weight accorded to an agency’s interpretation depends on factors like the thoroughness of the agency’s consideration, validity of its reasoning, consistency with earlier and later pronouncements, and other factors giving it persuasive power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both petitioners at oral argument embraced Skidmore; the author lists Skidmore’s enumerated factors as the classic non-binding 'weight' test. The post notes ambiguity in the majority opinion but records that parts of the opinion suggest some Skidmore-like respect for reasoned executive-branch interpretations.

rubrics_metrics.name: De novo (plenary) review/independent judgment as a possible replacement
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts may apply de novo review—exercising independent judgment without deferring to agency interpretations—as the replacement standard for reviewing agency statutory interpretations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Chief Justice's repeated references to 'independent judgment' suggest de novo review; the author finds the majority opinion ambiguous but leans toward an interpretation that de novo review is embraced, while recognizing some language leaves room for Skidmore-style weight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive-branch interpretations may inform but not control judicial judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts may give careful attention to the Executive Branch's judgments and seek aid from agency interpretations, but such attention only 'may inform' and does not obligate judicial deference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoted phrasing: 'Careful attention to the judgment of the Executive Branch may help inform that inquiry.' The post highlights that the majority permits courts to consider agency expertise and reasoned decisionmaking as informative, but stops short of requiring deference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constitutional argument that Chevron is unconstitutional
rubrics_metrics.description: Concurring views (Thomas and Gorsuch) argue Chevron is not only unlawful but unconstitutional, which would have implications if Congress attempted to codify Chevron.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Justice Gorsuch’s concurrence elaborates a historical/separation-of-powers case and argues stare decisis supports abandoning Chevron; the post notes the constitutional argument matters for whether Congress could later codify Chevron deference in statute.

rubrics_metrics.name: When statutes use broad open-ended terms, agencies may have policy discretion (State Farm-type approach)
rubrics_metrics.description: Statutes that use terms like 'reasonable,' 'appropriate,' 'feasible,' or 'practicable' afford agencies broad policy discretion; in such cases courts allow reasonable agency choices among textual options (more akin to arbitrary-and-capricious review than Chevron).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoting Justice Kavanaugh (from Kisor), the author notes this is more 'State Farm' than 'Chevron'—a reminder that agencies often have substantive discretion under broad statutory language and courts may evaluate reasonableness of agency policy choices rather than defer on pure legal questions.
